![Seven areal sub-regions and 292 catalogued census settlements across Cuba, Hispaniola, Jamaica and Puerto Rico from 1838 to 2025.](figures/greater_antilles_modern_regional_map.png)



# Abstract

Between the end of apprenticeship in the British West Indies in 1838 and the demographic contractions of the early twenty-first century, the four main islands of the Greater Antilles expanded nearly fifteenfold in aggregate population, moving from roughly 2,72M inhabitants in the early post-emancipation era to approximately 40,2M by 2025 under official national census benchmarks (and 36,95M inside the coarse coastal-gridded harmonisation footprint across 253.724 km²). Behind that shared Antillean climb lie five sharply divergent demographic transitions across 200.416 km² of surveyed island land [@Celade2020Observatorio; @Celade2024Observatorio]. Cuba advanced from 1,01M in 1841 and 1,57M in the 1899 post-war enumeration to 5,83M in 1953 and a peak of 11,17M in 2012, before sub-replacement fertility, rapid population ageing and post-2015 emigration initiated a sustained contraction [@USWarDeptCuba1900; @ONEICuba2014; @Song2023Aging]. On Hispaniola, Haiti climbed from roughly 380k in 1805 and 750k in 1838 to 3,1M in 1950, 8,37M in 2003 and 10,91M by 2015, sustaining dense rural smallholding alongside explosive metropolitan concentration across Port-au-Prince, Carrefour, Delmas and Pétionville even after the 2010 earthquake [@IHSIHaiti2015]. Across the border, the Dominican Republic rose from a sparsely settled frontier of roughly 135k in 1838 and 894,7k at its first modern census in 1920 to 10,77M in 2022, overtaking Cuba as the archipelago's leading metropolitan axis around Santo Domingo (2,75M) and Santiago de los Caballeros (612,6k) [@ONEDomRep2023; @MoyaPons1995]. Jamaica multiplied more than sevenfold from 377,4k in 1844 to 1,24M in 1943 and 2,7M in 2011 despite successive emigration waves to Panama, Britain and North America, while shifting urban gravity into Kingston and suburban Saint Catherine [@STATINJamaica2012; @Roberts1957]. Puerto Rico surged from 447,9k in 1846 and 953,2k in 1899 to a peak of 3,81M in 2000 under Operation Bootstrap and the Great Migration, before post-2006 fiscal contraction and Hurricane María drove a steep drop to 3,29M in 2020 [@USWarDeptPR1900; @VazquezCalzada1988; @USCensusPR2024]. Combining official national censuses, 25 sub-administrative enumeration benchmarks and a settlement gazetteer of 292 cities and towns (rank-size exponent $\alpha = 1,05$, $R^2 = 0,98$), this study reconstructs the divergent modern population trajectories of the Greater Antilles.

# Background

## Emancipation, Imperial Realignment and the Making of Five Antillean Regimes

The year 1838 marks a clean watershed across the Greater Antilles, though it did not arrive simultaneously on every shore. On 1 August 1838, the termination of apprenticeship across the British Caribbean ended legal bondage in Jamaica, inaugurating the archipelago's first continuous series of post-emancipation censuses in 1844 [@Roberts1957; @STATINJamaica2012]. Haiti had already abolished slavery four decades earlier in the Haitian Revolution of 1791 to 1804, emerging from catastrophic war losses with barely 380k inhabitants in 1805 and remaining locked out of Atlantic plantation finance until its rural peasantry consolidated on fragmented highland plots [@IHSIHaiti2015]. The eastern two-thirds of Hispaniola, sparsely peopled by cattle ranchers and smallholders, threw off Haitian administration in 1844 to establish the Dominican Republic with scarcely 135k inhabitants, leaving an extraordinary demographic asymmetry across the island's mountain frontier [@MoyaPons1995].

In the Spanish Antilles, by contrast, emancipation arrived nearly half a century later. Puerto Rico abolished slavery in 1873 while already possessing a dense free *jíbaro* peasantry in the central cordillera and a growing coastal sugar labour force [@VazquezCalzada1988]. Cuba held onto plantation slavery until 1886, importing hundreds of thousands of enslaved Africans alongside Chinese indentured labourers and Spanish peninsular migrants to feed its mechanised central-and-western sugar belt [@USWarDeptCuba1900; @DiazBriquets1983]. Only after the Spanish-American War of 1898 severed Madrid's last American possessions did Cuba and Puerto Rico enter the twentieth century under radically altered constitutional frameworks: Cuba as an independent republic deeply linked to North American capital, and Puerto Rico as an unincorporated United States territory whose residents acquired statutory United States citizenship in 1917 [@USWarDeptPR1900; @VazquezCalzada1988].

Out of these distinct nineteenth-century starting lines grew five contrasting modern demographic regimes. No other archipelago of comparable size exhibits such wide divergence in fertility timing, mortality decline, cross-border migration and metropolitan structure. Within two hundred kilometres across the Windward Passage and Mona Passage, late-twentieth-century Cuba and Puerto Rico converged on European-style below-replacement fertility and rapid population ageing, Jamaica moderated its natural increase through persistent transnational emigration, the Dominican Republic completed a brisk mid-century frontier boom and rapid urban transition, and Haiti sustained the Western Hemisphere's last prolonged high-fertility rural expansion [@Celade2020Observatorio; @Celade2024Observatorio].

## Cuba: Immigration Waves, the Health Revolution and Early Demographic Ageing

At the close of Spanish rule, Cuba was still a land-abundant island whose population had been severely pruned by the Ten Years' War (1868 to 1878) and the War of Independence (1895 to 1898). The United States War Department census of 1899 enumerated 1.572.797 inhabitants across the island's six historical provinces, recording stark demographic scars in Matanzas, Santa Clara and Havana where General Valeriano Weyler's *reconcentración* policy had elevated civilian mortality [@USWarDeptCuba1900]. Yet peace, sanitary campaigns against yellow fever and malaria, and an immense wave of Atlantic and Caribbean immigration swiftly reversed the war deficit [@DiazBriquets1983]. Between 1900 and 1930, more than one million immigrants landed in Cuban ports: primarily Galicians, Asturians and Canary Islanders settling across western and central Cuba, joined during the sugar boom of the 1910s and 1920s by tens of thousands of Haitian and Jamaican *braceros* cutting cane across the newly cleared *latifundia* of Camagüey and Oriente [@ONEICuba2014; @DiazBriquets1983].

By the 1953 national census, Cuba's population had nearly quadrupled since 1899 to 5.829.029, with Western Cuba anchored on Havana (785,5k city proper in 1953) holding 2,38M inhabitants, Central Cuba 1,65M and Eastern Cuba (Oriente) 1,8M [@ONEICuba2014]. Mortality had already fallen dramatically well before 1959, driven by urban waterworks, vector control and expanding medical access [@DiazBriquets1983]. Following the 1959 revolution, universal primary health care, rural clinics, female educational expansion and legalised fertility control compressed both infant mortality and birth rates at remarkable speed [@DiazBriquets1983; @Garcia2024Mortalidad]. After a brief post-revolutionary baby boom during the early 1960s and repeated waves of emigration to Florida—first in 1959 to 1962, then via the Camarioca and Freedom Flights, the 1980 Mariel boatlift and the 1994 *balsero* crisis—Cuba's total fertility rate dropped below replacement level in 1978, decades ahead of the rest of Latin America [@Celade2019Observatorio; @Song2023Aging].

National headcount slowed steadily thereafter, rising from 9,72M in 1981 to 11,18M in 2002 and plateauing at 11,17M (11.167.325) in the 2012 census [@ONEICuba2014]. In the twenty-first century, Cuba entered an advanced post-transitional regime characterised by an inverted age pyramid, rising chronic cardiovascular disease burden and pronounced internal migration of older residents toward Havana and provincial capitals [@Hiortlorenzen2015Envejecimiento; @Collazoramos2016Algunas; @Rodriguez2015Envejecimiento; @Herrera2019Mortalidad]. Even as urban child-health cohorts in Havana and district-level infant mortality monitoring in Santiago de Cuba demonstrated sustained clinical surveillance despite material scarcity [@Britton2020Prevalence; @Garcia2024Mortalidad], accelerating post-2015 and post-2021 out-migration combined with persistent low fertility pulled Cuba's resident population into absolute contraction [@Song2023Aging; @Celade2024Observatorio].

## Hispaniola Divided: Haitian Peasant Density and Dominican Frontier Expansion

Hispaniola presents the starkest demographic reversal in the Caribbean. Throughout the nineteenth century, Haiti held the overwhelming share of the island's population. Emerging from independence with roughly 380k survivors in 1805, Haiti recovered steadily through natural increase among free rural smallholders who rejected plantation wage labour in favour of subsistence *lakou* compounds and coffee cultivation across the Massif de la Hotte, the Artibonite valley and the northern plains. By 1838, Haiti held approximately 750k inhabitants—more than five times the population of the neighbouring Dominican territory—and reached roughly 1,28M by 1900 [@IHSIHaiti2015].

Haiti's first modern national census, conducted in 1950 by the Institut Haïtien de Statistique et d'Informatique (IHSI), recorded 3.097.220 inhabitants across an overwhelmingly agrarian landscape in which Port-au-Prince still counted just 134,1k residents [@IHSIHaiti2015]. Over the subsequent half-century, declining childhood mortality without commensurate industrial employment or rapid fertility reduction propelled explosive growth: population climbed to 4,31M in 1971, 5,05M in 1982, 8,37M (8.373.750) in 2003 and an IHSI departmental estimate of 10,91M in 2015, approaching 11,9M by 2025 [@IHSIHaiti2015; @Celade2020Observatorio]. Rural ecological strain, soil erosion and deforestation across the southern and northwestern peninsulas pushed hundreds of thousands of migrants either overseas—into the Dominican Republic, the Bahamas, the United States and maritime refuge flows such as the 1981 to 1982 Fort Allen detention cohort in Puerto Rico [@Cabral1995Migracio; @Santos2025Decolonizing; @Celade2019Observatorio]—or into the metropolitan basin of the Ouest department. Port-au-Prince's municipal core grew from 134,1k in 1950 to 876k by 2009, while its surrounding communes of Carrefour (430,3k), Delmas (359,5k), Pétionville (271,2k) and Cité Soleil (241,1k) expanded into a sprawling conurbation exceeding two million residents that absorbed the devastating mortality and displacement shock of the January 2010 earthquake [@IHSIHaiti2015].

East of the Massacre and Artibonite headwaters, the Dominican Republic followed a profoundly different trajectory. Following independence in 1844 and the War of Restoration (1863 to 1865), the republic possessed vast tracts of fertile, lightly settled land across the Cibao valley and the eastern plains [@MoyaPons1995]. Modern sugar plantations established by Cuban and North American capital around San Pedro de Macorís and La Romana in the late nineteenth century, alongside tobacco and cacao smallholding around Santiago de los Caballeros, initiated brisk growth. The first national census of 1920 enumerated 894.665 inhabitants—still well under half of Haiti's population—with Santo Domingo holding only 31k residents [@ONEDomRep2023; @MoyaPons1995]. Thereafter, frontier colonisation, road building, public sanitation and sustained cross-border Haitian labour migration into sugar *bateyes*, construction and agriculture accelerated demographic expansion [@Cabral1995Migracio; @MoyaPons1995]. Total population reached 2,14M in 1950, 5,65M in 1981, 8,56M in 2002 and 10,77M in the tenth national census of 2022 [@ONEDomRep2023]. Unlike Haiti's rural density, Dominican growth became decisively metropolitan and coastal-industrial: Greater Santo Domingo expanded to 2,75M inside the main urban agglomeration (with Distrito Nacional and Santo Domingo province together surpassing 3,8M), Santiago de los Caballeros reached 612,6k, and eastern tourism and industrial corridors propelled La Romana (265,3k), Higüey (210,3k) and San Pedro de Macorís (207,4k) while national fertility converged steadily toward replacement [@ONEDomRep2023; @Cernigliaro2018Factors; @Celade2024Observatorio].

## Jamaica and Puerto Rico: Free Villages, Diaspora Circuits and Post-Industrial Contraction

Jamaica and Puerto Rico illustrate two distinct insular pathways in which metropolitan ties to imperial powers shaped every decade of modern demographic change. Immediately after full emancipation in 1838, formerly enslaved Jamaicans left coastal sugar estates in large numbers to establish Baptist- and Moravian-assisted free villages across the interior limestone parishes of Manchester, Clarendon, Saint Ann and Saint Elizabeth [@Roberts1957]. Jamaica's 1844 census counted 377.433 inhabitants, with Kingston holding 32,9k and the old administrative capital Spanish Town just 5,8k [@STATINJamaica2012; @Roberts1957]. As plantation revenues weakened in the late nineteenth century, Jamaican labourers became the premier mobile workforce of the circum-Caribbean, migrating in tens of thousands to build the Panama railway and Panama Canal, harvest bananas in Costa Rica and Honduras, and cut cane in eastern Cuba [@Roberts1957]. Despite that outflow, falling mortality lifted Jamaica from 831,4k in 1911 to 1,24M in 1943 and 1,61M on the eve of independence in 1960 [@STATINJamaica2012].

From the late 1940s onward, the Windrush migration to the United Kingdom—followed after 1965 by heavy family-reunification and skilled-worker flows to the United States and Canada—acted as a durable demographic safety valve, syphoning off a large fraction of Jamaica's natural increase and anchoring a vigorous transnational diaspora [@Roberts1957; @Bourne2026Black; @Celade2019Observatorio]. Domestic growth moderated accordingly, climbing from 1,86M in 1970 to 2,61M in 2001 and 2,7M in 2011 (reaching 2,77M in provisional post-2020 series), while urban population poured out of central Kingston into Saint Andrew (583,7k) and the planned suburban dormitory towns of Portmore (182,2k peak in 2011) and Spanish Town (168,9k) in Saint Catherine parish [@STATINJamaica2012]. Immediately to Jamaica's northwest, its former dependency of the Cayman Islands—administered from Kingston until 1962—shifted from a tiny seafaring outpost of 5,5k residents in 1911 to a booming offshore financial centre of 71,1k inhabitants by 2021, driven largely by expatriate immigration [@ESOCayman2022].

Puerto Rico experienced the most dramatic boom-and-bust demographic arc in the modern Antilles. Under Spanish rule, high natural increase lifted the island from 447.914 inhabitants in 1846 to 953.243 in the United States War Department census of 1899, distributed densely across highland coffee municipios and coastal sugar plains while San Juan held just 32k inhabitants [@USWarDeptPR1900; @VazquezCalzada1988]. Following 1898, American public-health campaigns against hookworm, malaria and tuberculosis cut death rates sharply, pushing population past 1,54M in 1930 and 2,21M in 1950 [@VazquezCalzada1988]. From the late 1940s through the 1960s, Governor Luis Muñoz Marín's Operation Bootstrap (*Manos a la Obra*) transformed an agrarian island into a light-manufacturing and pharmaceutical hub while cheap air links carried over half a million Puerto Ricans to New York, Chicago and Philadelphia during the Great Migration [@VazquezCalzada1988; @USCensusPR2024]. Return flows and suburban expansion nonetheless carried the island's population to an all-time decennial peak of 3.808.610 in 2000, centred on Greater San Juan and its populous inner suburbs of Bayamón (203,5k urban peak in 2000), Carolina (168,2k), Caguas (92,4k) and Guaynabo (78,8k) [@Bureau2012Census; @USCensusPR2024]. Once federal Section 936 industrial tax incentives expired in 2006, however, a decade-long fiscal crisis collided with collapsing fertility and the catastrophic landfall of Hurricane María in September 2017. Census population fell to 3,73M in 2010 and tumbled by nearly 12% to 3,29M (3.285.874) in 2020—with San Juan city proper shrinking from its 1970 peak of 452,7k to 322,9k—marking the sharpest peacetime demographic contraction of any major Greater Antillean jurisdiction [@Bureau2012Census; @USCensusPR2024; @Celade2024Observatorio].

# Methodology

## Territorial Mask Architecture and Sub-Regional Partition

To analyse demographic divergence without masking Cuba's pronounced internal east-west gradient, JAGUAR partitions the Greater Antilles into seven contiguous territorial sub-regions covering 200.416 km² of surveyed island land (and 253.724 km² inside the 5-arc-minute coastal raster mask across 3.152 gridded cells). Cuba—which accounts for slightly more than half of the archipelago's land area—is divided into three administrative macro-zones aligned with official ONEI provincial boundaries: Western Cuba (Havana, Artemisa, Mayabeque, Pinar del Río, Matanzas and Isla de la Juventud; 30.959 km² surveyed land), Central Cuba (Villa Clara, Cienfuegos, Sancti Spíritus, Ciego de Ávila and Camagüey; 40.346 km²) and Eastern Cuba or Oriente (Las Tunas, Holguín, Granma, Santiago de Cuba and Guantánamo; 34.890 km²) [@ONEICuba2014]. The remaining four jurisdictions form single island or national masks: Haiti (27.828 km²), the Dominican Republic (47.058 km²), Jamaica (10.749 km²) and Puerto Rico (8.584 km²).

This seven-part geometry captures the decisive geographic contrasts of the modern Antilles: the early concentration of Cuban capital, port trade and European immigration in Western Cuba versus the twentieth-century sugar frontier of Camagüey and Oriente; the abrupt ecological and institutional border dividing mountainous Haiti from the broader alluvial valleys of the Dominican Republic; and the compact island constraints of Jamaica and Puerto Rico, where metropolitan sprawl rapidly engulfed narrow coastal plains [@MoyaPons1995; @Roberts1957; @VazquezCalzada1988].

## Official Census Reconciliation and Inter-Censal Growth Modelling

Unlike pre-modern chapters that rely on archaeological proxies or colonial tribute multipliers, the Greater Antilles between 1838 and 2025 belong squarely to the modern statistical census regime. Primary population series are anchored directly to published national enumerations: the 1841, 1861, 1899 and 1907 to 2012 censuses of Cuba [@USWarDeptCuba1900; @ONEICuba2014]; the 1846, 1899 and 1910 to 2020 decennial censuses plus Vintage 2023 municipio estimates of Puerto Rico [@USWarDeptPR1900; @Bureau2012Census; @USCensusPR2024]; the 1844 to 2011 censuses of Jamaica and 1911 to 2021 censuses of the Cayman Islands [@STATINJamaica2012; @Roberts1957; @ESOCayman2022]; the 1920 to 2022 national censuses of the Dominican Republic [@ONEDomRep2023]; and the 1950 to 2003 national censuses plus 2015 departmental projections of Haiti [@IHSIHaiti2015].

For any sub-region $r$ observed at consecutive census dates $t_1$ and $t_2$, inter-censal population change obeys the fundamental demographic balancing identity:

$$P_r(t_2) = P_r(t_1) + B_r(t_1, t_2) - D_r(t_1, t_2) + M_r^{\mathrm{in}}(t_1, t_2) - M_r^{\mathrm{out}}(t_1, t_2)$$

where $B_r$ and $D_r$ denote cumulative births and deaths and $M_r^{\mathrm{in}} - M_r^{\mathrm{out}}$ captures net internal and international migration [@Celade2019Observatorio; @Celade2020Observatorio]. Compound annual growth rates between census benchmarks follow standard geometric compounding:

$$g_r(t_1, t_2) = \left(\frac{P_r(t_2)}{P_r(t_1)}\right)^{\frac{1}{t_2 - t_1}} - 1$$

In the modern Greater Antilles, the migration term $M_r^{\mathrm{in}} - M_r^{\mathrm{out}}$ frequently rivals or overrides natural increase $B_r - D_r$. In early twentieth-century Cuba, positive net immigration lifted annual growth above 2,5% per year, whereas in post-1950 Jamaica, post-2006 Puerto Rico and post-2015 Cuba, sustained negative net migration depressed or inverted population growth even while life expectancy exceeded 75 years [@DiazBriquets1983; @VazquezCalzada1988; @Song2023Aging; @Celade2024Observatorio].

## Gazetteer Compilation, Metropolitan Scope and Rank-Size Scaling

Alongside sub-regional totals, JAGUAR assembles an evidence-only urban gazetteer of 292 settlements across the five Greater Antillean polities spanning 1841 to 2022, with zero crowd-sourced entries (0% fallback share). Four sequential ingestion waves tracked in the chapter source ledger consolidated 267 settlements from primary national census tables (Wave 1), 19 from demographic monographs and peer-reviewed historical compilations (Wave 2), 4 from longitudinal census backfill (Wave 3) and 2 from sub-regional coverage verification sweeps (Wave 4), yielding a final marginal gain of 0,69% and complete coverage across all seven sub-regions: 85 settlements in Puerto Rico, 61 in the Dominican Republic sub-region (64 under national borders due to three border-adjacent towns), 56 in Jamaica, 33 in the Haiti sub-region (30 under national borders), 21 in Eastern Cuba, 19 in Central Cuba and 17 in Western Cuba.

To prevent double-counting metropolitan agglomerations against their constituent commuter municipalities, every settlement carries an explicit urban-scope classification: 275 standalone cities and towns alongside 17 explicitly tagged suburban municipalities linked to their parent capitals—four around Port-au-Prince (Carrefour, Delmas, Cité Soleil and Croix-des-Bouquets), nine around San Juan (Bayamón, Carolina, Caguas, Guaynabo, Trujillo Alto, Cataño, Canóvanas, Toa Alta and Toa Baja), two around Kingston (Portmore and Spanish Town) and two around Santo Domingo (Boca Chica and Bajos de Haina). Urban hierarchy concentration across all 292 settlements is evaluated through an ordinary least-squares log-log rank-size regression fitted over the upper 146 settlements:

$$\log_{10} P_{(k)} = \log_{10} P_{(1)} - \alpha \log_{10} k$$

where $P_{(k)}$ is the peak recorded population of the $k$-th ranked settlement and $\alpha$ measures urban concentration around Zipf's benchmark of unity [@ONEDomRep2023; @ONEICuba2014].

# Testing and Validation

## Census-to-Raster Cross-Checks and Sub-Regional Plausibility

Rigorous testing in a multi-island census chapter requires reconciling two distinct statistical layers: the official sub-regional census benchmarks compiled from primary national statistical offices and the 5-arc-minute gridded dasymetric raster series extracted across the regional polygon masks. Comparing the official census series against the 5-arc-minute gridded raster extractions in Table \ref{tab:raster-comparison} uncovers two informative spatial artefacts that must be explicitly understood before reading the gridded trajectory plots. First, because 5-arc-minute cells straddle ragged coastlines, cays and narrow bays across all four islands, the rasterised mask footprint totals 253.724 km²—roughly 26,6% wider than the 200.416 km² surveyed land area—reducing raw gridded densities across narrow or deeply indented masks such as Puerto Rico (12.726 km² raster footprint versus 8.584 km² land area) and Western Cuba (42.613 km² versus 30.959 km²). Second, historical sub-administrative regime handoffs in the gridded reconstruction introduce discrete step adjustments when national census grids supersede nineteenth-century interpolations (at 1920 in the Dominican Republic, 1930 in Jamaica, 1955 to 1956 in Cuba and Haiti, and 1975 in Puerto Rico) and clip narrow littoral cores around Havana Bay and San Juan Harbour, depressing gridded 2025 totals for Western Cuba (2,36M raster versus 4,32M census) and Puerto Rico (1,09M raster versus 3,21M census) while tracking Eastern Cuba (3,89M versus 3,76M), Central Cuba (2,53M versus 2,74M), Haiti (11,24M versus 11,9M) and Jamaica (2,77M versus 2,84M) closely.

## Sub-Administrative Historical GIS Verification

To guard against national-level aggregation error, JAGUAR validates sub-regional totals against 25 primary sub-administrative census enumerations scraped across historical Cuban provinces, Puerto Rican historic departments, pre- and post-1982 Haitian departments, Dominican provinces and Jamaican parishes (Table \ref{tab:hgis-subadmin}). These primary sub-national tallies confirm the structural geography visible in the regional tables: by 1970, Oriente (3M) had already overtaken La Habana province (2,34M) as Cuba's most populous historical province [@ONEICuba2014]; in Puerto Rico, the historic Bayamón-San Juan northern department (1,1M) dwarfed Guayama (394,7k), Ponce (359,3k), Arecibo (266k) and Mayagüez (216,9k) [@USCensusPR2024]; in Haiti, the Ouest department surged from 1,67M in 1971 to 4,03M in 2015 while Artibonite reached 1,73M and Nord 1,07M [@IHSIHaiti2015]; in the Dominican Republic, Distrito Nacional and Santo Domingo province dominated ahead of Santiago (1,07M in 2022), San Cristóbal (688,8k) and the rapidly expanding eastern tourist province of La Altagracia (446,1k) [@ONEDomRep2023]; and in Jamaica, Saint Andrew (583,7k) and Saint Catherine (542,8k) together held over two-fifths of the island's residents in 2022 [@STATINJamaica2012].

# Results

## Archipelagic Demographic Trajectory (1838 to 2025)

Across nearly two centuries of post-emancipation history, the Greater Antilles expanded from approximately 2,72M inhabitants around 1841 to 4,76M by 1900, 15,01M by 1953, 35,34M by 2002 and 40,2M by 2025 on the official census benchmark series—a 14,8-fold expansion that lifted mean surveyed island density from 13,6 to 200,6 inhabitants per km² [@Celade2020Observatorio; @Celade2024Observatorio]. Inside the gridded raster series plotted in Figure \ref{fig:ga-trajectory}, aggregate regional headcount climbs from 805,6k in 1840 and 1,42M in 1900 to 17,02M in 1960, 24,57M in 1980, 30,54M in 2000 and 36,95M in 2025, clearly registering the post-1980 divergence between rapidly growing Hispaniola and flattening or contracting Cuba and Puerto Rico.

<figure class="crd-figure-block" id="fig:ga-trajectory">
<img class="crd-figure-img" src="/artefacts/project_jaguar/1.0-greater-antilles-modern/greater_antilles_modern_population_trajectory.png" alt="fig:ga-trajectory" loading="lazy" />
<figcaption class="crd-caption"><span class="crd-caption-label">Figure 2.</span> Gridded population trajectories for the Greater Antilles and its four largest sub-regions from 1840 to 2025 (Panel A) and sub-regional gridded densities in 2025 (Panel B).</figcaption>
</figure>

The long-term redistribution of population across the four main islands constitutes one of the sharpest geopolitical shifts in the Americas. Around 1841, Cuba (1,01M, 37% of the Greater Antilles) and Haiti (750k, 27,6%) dominated the archipelago, trailed by Puerto Rico (447,9k, 16,5%) and Jamaica (377,4k, 13,9%), while the Dominican Republic trailed far behind at roughly 135k (5%). By 1953, following half a century of Cuban immigration and sanitary reform, Cuba still led decisively with 5,83M inhabitants (38,8% of the archipelago), ahead of Haiti (3,1M in 1950, rising to roughly 3,31M by 1953), Puerto Rico (2,27M), the Dominican Republic (2,31M) and Jamaica (1,43M).

By 2025, that mid-century hierarchy had been turned upside down. Hispaniola—split almost evenly between Haiti (11,9M benchmark; 11,24M gridded) and the Dominican Republic (11,43M benchmark; 13,08M gridded)—accounted for 58% of the entire Greater Antillean census population (23,33M of 40,2M). Cuba's share contracted from 38,8% in 1953 to 26,9% in 2025 (10,82M benchmark, and falling further under post-2021 emigration), while Puerto Rico's share halved from 15,1% in 1953 to 8% in 2025 (3,21M) and Jamaica eased to 7,1% (2,84M). Density contrasts widened in parallel: on surveyed land area, Haiti reached 427,6 inhabitants per km² (327,1 in the wider raster mask) and Puerto Rico still carried 373,4 inhabitants per km² despite two decades of depopulation, ahead of Jamaica (264,2), the Dominican Republic (242,9) and Cuba (101,9 overall, ranging from 139,5 in Western Cuba down to 67,9 in Central Cuba).

## Cuba's Three-Zone Internal Balance and Twenty-First-Century Contraction

Within Cuba, modern demographic history unfolded as a long eastward drift followed by metropolitan stabilisation and late-century ageing. At the 1841 Spanish census, Western Cuba held more than half the island's population (520k of 1,01M, or 51,6%), sustained by the port primacy of Havana (137,5k) and the dense sugar estates of Matanzas and Güines [@USWarDeptCuba1900]. By 1899, after wartime devastation in the west and early rail expansion into Santa Clara and Camagüey, Western Cuba's share stood at 50,8% (798k of 1,57M), while Central Cuba rose to 28,3% (445k) and Eastern Cuba held 20,9% (329k) [@USWarDeptCuba1900].

The decisive shift occurred between 1900 and 1953. Massive North American capital investment cleared virgin forests across Camagüey and northern Oriente for central sugar mills, drawing both internal Cuban migrants and tens of thousands of Antillean seasonal labourers [@DiazBriquets1983; @ONEICuba2014]. Eastern Cuba expanded more than fivefold from 329k in 1899 to 1,8M in 1953 (30,9% of Cuba), while Central Cuba rose nearly fourfold to 1,65M (28,3%) and Western Cuba's share declined to 40,8% (2,38M), even as Havana itself climbed from 236k in 1899 to 785,5k in 1953 [@ONEICuba2014].

After 1959, revolutionary regional policy deliberately redirected housing, industrial estates and health infrastructure toward provincial capitals outside Havana—above all Santiago de Cuba (rising from 163,2k in 1953 to 431,4k in 2022), Camagüey (110,4k to 310,8k), Holguín (57,6k to 302,9k), Santa Clara (to 217,9k), Guantánamo (peak 217,1k in 2012), Las Tunas (176,1k) and Bayamo (159k) [@ONEICuba2014]. Havana's share of national population was effectively capped, with the capital peaking at 2.201.610 in 2002 before edging down to 2.106.146 in 2012 and 2.137.847 in 2022 official registers [@ONEICuba2014]. Meanwhile, Cuba's exceptionally early fertility transition—coupled with sustained life expectancy gains and rising chronic cardiovascular mortality among older cohorts—turned the entire island into the oldest society in Latin America [@DiazBriquets1983; @Collazoramos2016Algunas; @Herrera2019Mortalidad]. By the 2010s, elderly internal mobility toward Havana and western provincial capitals coexisted with sharp rural emptying across Villa Clara, Sancti Spíritus and Matanzas, while youth emigration accelerated sharply after 2015, pushing every Cuban sub-region below its early-2000s peak [@Hiortlorenzen2015Envejecimiento; @Rodriguez2015Envejecimiento; @Song2023Aging; @Britton2020Prevalence; @Garcia2024Mortalidad].

## Hispaniola: Divergent Urbanisation across a Shared Island

Hispaniola's two republics demonstrate how identical tropical island geographies can yield utterly contrasting settlement systems when governed by different land-tenure and capital regimes. In Haiti, nineteenth-century agrarian egalitarianism produced one of the densest peasant countrysides in the Americas, keeping urbanisation remarkably low until the second half of the twentieth century. As late as 1950, barely one-tenth of Haiti's 3,1M inhabitants lived in towns; Port-au-Prince counted 134,1k residents, Cap-Haïtien 24,2k and Gonaïves just 13,6k [@IHSIHaiti2015].

Between 1950 and 2015, however, declining agricultural yields, rural land fragmentation and centralised fiscal administration in the capital triggered a dramatic urban implosion toward the Cul-de-Sac plain. Port-au-Prince city proper multiplied six-and-a-half times to 876k by 2009, while its contiguous metropolitan communes exploded out of peripheral fields and hillsides: Carrefour jumped from 129,5k in 1982 to 430,3k in 2009, Pétionville surged nearly eightfold from 35,3k to 271,2k, and Delmas (359,5k), Cité Soleil (241,1k) and Croix-des-Bouquets (84,8k) formed an uninterrupted belt around the bay [@IHSIHaiti2015]. Secondary coastal ports expanded far more modestly, led by Gonaïves (228,7k in 2009), Cap-Haïtien (155,5k), Saint-Marc (122,7k) and Les Cayes (71,2k). The magnitude-7 earthquake of 12 January 2010 inflicted catastrophic casualties across Port-au-Prince, Léogâne (86k) and Jacmel, temporarily dispersing hundreds of thousands of survivors into provincial communes before rapid informal re-densification resumed in the Ouest department, alongside ongoing emigration to the Dominican Republic, Puerto Rico and North America [@IHSIHaiti2015; @Santos2025Decolonizing; @Celade2019Observatorio].

Across the border, the Dominican Republic achieved equally rapid aggregate growth—multiplying twelvefold from 894,7k in 1920 to 10,77M in 2022—yet channelled that expansion into a balanced twin-corridor urban network supported by agricultural modernisation, free-zone manufacturing and mass coastal tourism [@ONEDomRep2023; @MoyaPons1995]. Santo Domingo grew nearly ninetyfold over a century, leaping from 31k in 1920 and 181,6k in 1950 to 1,31M in 1981, 1,89M in 2002 and 2,75M in 2022, flanked by industrial and coastal suburbs at Boca Chica (76k) and Bajos de Haina (75,8k) and the adjacent provincial capital San Cristóbal (167,5k) [@ONEDomRep2023]. Inland, the fertile Cibao valley sustained a vigorous secondary hierarchy headed by Santiago de los Caballeros (rising from 17,2k in 1920 to 612,6k in 2022), San Francisco de Macorís (132,7k), La Vega (123,7k), Moca (71k) and Bonao (72,2k). On the southeastern littoral, sugar plantations originally staffed by cross-border Haitian and Anglophone *cocolo* workers [@Cabral1995Migracio] gave way to resort and logistics hubs around La Romana (265,3k), San Pedro de Macorís (207,4k), Higüey (210,3k) and Punta Cana (100k). Fertility declined rapidly after 1970 as female schooling and urban employment expanded, though regional reproductive health studies confirm persistent socioeconomic gradients in maternal care and family-size preferences across urban and peri-urban districts [@Cernigliaro2018Factors; @Celade2024Observatorio].

## Jamaica and Puerto Rico: Diaspora Safety Valves and Post-Industrial Reversal

Jamaica's modern demographic path stands as the archetype of migration-moderated island transition. Between 1844 (377,4k) and 1911 (831,4k), population grew at 1,19% per year despite recurrent cholera outbreaks in 1850 to 1851 and massive male out-migration to the Panama Canal works [@Roberts1957; @STATINJamaica2012]. Between 1911 and 1960, falling infant mortality lifted annual growth to 1,36% per year, carrying Jamaica to 1,61M on the eve of independence, even as post-war Windrush emigration sent over 160k Jamaicans to Britain during the 1950s and early 1960s [@Roberts1957; @Bourne2026Black]. After 1960, sustained emigration to the United States and Canada alongside steady fertility decline slowed aggregate growth sharply: Jamaica added 1M people between 1960 and 2001 (1,18% per year), then barely 90k between 2001 and 2011 (0,34% per year, reaching 2,7M) [@STATINJamaica2012; @Celade2020Observatorio]. Inside the island, rural-to-urban migration reshaped the southern Liguanea Plain: Kingston expanded from 32,9k in 1844 to 109,1k in 1943 and 611,2k by 2022 (combining the Kingston and urban Saint Andrew corporate core), while planned middle- and working-class sprawl turned Portmore from 5,1k residents in 1970 into 182,2k by 2011 (161,4k in 2022) and lifted historic Spanish Town to 168,9k, accompanied by secondary nodes at Montego Bay (110,1k), May Pen (72,2k) and Mandeville (55k) [@STATINJamaica2012]. Across the western sea channel, the Cayman Islands diverged into a high-immigration micro-polity rising from 5,5k in 1911 and 10,1k in 1970 to 71,1k by 2021 [@ESOCayman2022].

Puerto Rico's twentieth-century rise and twenty-first-century reversal are unmatched in statistical clarity across the Caribbean. From 953,2k inhabitants in 1899, natural increase lifted the island to 1,87M by 1940 and 2,21M by 1950 despite accelerating migration to the mainland United States [@USWarDeptPR1900; @VazquezCalzada1988]. During the Operation Bootstrap decades (1950 to 1980), massive out-migration—peaking at over 45k net departures annually in the mid-1950s—capped decennial growth at just 6,3% in the 1950s (2,35M in 1960) before industrial expansion and return migration lifted headcount to 2,71M in 1970, 3,2M in 1980, 3,52M in 1990 and the historical ceiling of 3,81M in 2000 [@VazquezCalzada1988; @USCensusPR2024]. Urbanisation simultaneously hollowed out the interior coffee mountains and consolidated a sprawling northern metropolitan arc: San Juan proper peaked at 452,7k in 1970 before suburban flight expanded Bayamón (203,5k urban peak in 2000), Carolina (168,2k), Caguas (92,4k), Guaynabo (78,8k) and Trujillo Alto (50,8k), while southern Ponce peaked at 159,2k in 1990 and western Mayagüez at 83k [@Bureau2012Census; @USCensusPR2024]. After 2006, recession, public debt restructuring, ultra-low fertility (falling below 1 child per woman) and Hurricane María reversed a century of growth: population fell by 2,2% between 2000 and 2010 (to 3,73M) and plunged by 11,8% between 2010 and 2020 (to 3,29M), shrinking San Juan to 322,9k, Ponce to 108k and Carolina to 138,3k and leaving Puerto Rico alongside Cuba at the forefront of Antillean demographic contraction [@Bureau2012Census; @USCensusPR2024; @Celade2024Observatorio].

## Greater Antillean Urban Hierarchy and Zipf Scaling

Across all 292 catalogued towns and cities, the Greater Antilles display a remarkably well-ordered urban hierarchy that closely mirrors classical Zipfian scaling (Figure \ref{fig:ga-hierarchy}). Fitted across the upper 146 settlements of the 292-entry register, the log-log rank-size slope yields $\alpha = 1,05$ with $R^2 = 0,98$, sitting almost directly on Zipf's canonical benchmark of $\alpha = 1,0$. Unlike continental Latin American nations dominated by a single hyper-primate megacity, the four-island political partition of the Greater Antilles produces a multi-polar upper tier: two multi-million national capitals (Santo Domingo at 2,75M and La Habana at 2,2M peak), a cluster of mid-tier capitals and major secondary centres between 400k and 900k (Port-au-Prince city proper at 876k, Santiago de los Caballeros at 612,6k, Kingston at 611,2k, San Juan at 452,7k peak, Santiago de Cuba at 431,4k and Carrefour at 430,3k) and a dense middle rank of provincial capitals and metropolitan suburbs spanning 100k to 360k.

Table \ref{tab:top20-cities} compiles the 20 largest catalogued settlements across the Greater Antilles, documenting their polity, urban-scope designation, earliest and latest census figures, peak population and peak year. Notice how metropolitan morphology diverges sharply across the five polities: Santo Domingo and La Habana consolidate their primary urban populations within expansive central jurisdictions, whereas Port-au-Prince (with Carrefour, Delmas and Cité Soleil in the top 14 alone), San Juan (flanked by Bayamón and Carolina) and Kingston (flanked by Portmore and Spanish Town just outside the top 20) distribute a huge share of their functional urban populations across legally distinct suburban municipalities [@IHSIHaiti2015; @Bureau2012Census; @STATINJamaica2012; @ONEDomRep2023; @ONEICuba2014].

# Limitations

Four concrete statistical and cartographic constraints govern modern demographic synthesis across the Greater Antilles.

First, national census periodicity and archival continuity remain uneven across the five polities. Puerto Rico and Jamaica possess uninterrupted modern decennial series extending back to 1899 and 1844 respectively [@USWarDeptPR1900; @STATINJamaica2012], and Cuba and the Dominican Republic maintain high-grade national enumerations across the twentieth and early twenty-first centuries [@ONEICuba2014; @ONEDomRep2023]. Haiti, however, did not conduct a full national census until 1950 and has executed none since 2003, forcing post-2003 national, departmental and municipal series—including all post-2010 earthquake demographic reconstructions—to rely on IHSI projections and household-survey updates rather than a fresh complete count [@IHSIHaiti2015]. Similarly, Cuba postponed its scheduled 2022 national census amid severe post-pandemic economic strain and rapid unrecorded emigration, meaning that post-2020 official population registers likely overstate Cuba's de facto resident headcount by several hundred thousand inhabitants [@Song2023Aging; @Celade2024Observatorio].

Second, municipal versus urbanised-area boundary definitions introduce apparent jumps in city-proper time series. In Jamaica, Kingston's jump from 123,4k in 1960 to 473,7k in 1970 reflects the statistical consolidation of urban Saint Andrew with old Kingston parish rather than an instantaneous fourfold influx [@STATINJamaica2012]. In Puerto Rico, United States Census Bureau PL 94-171 urban-place boundaries separate central *pueblo* tracts from wider *municipio* boundaries, causing Bayamón's core *pueblo* tract to register just 1,9k in 2020 against a 2000 *zona urbana* peak of 203,5k even while Bayamón *municipio* as a whole remained above 185k residents [@Bureau2012Census; @USCensusPR2024]. Cross-border metropolitan comparisons therefore pair city-proper counts with explicitly tagged suburban municipalities and provincial benchmarks.

Third, cross-border migration across Hispaniola and maritime emigration across the Straits of Florida and Mona Passage resist exact annual accounting. Undocumented Haitian residents and Dominican-born descendants of Haitian migrants inside the Dominican Republic have long been subject to fluctuating civil-registration rules and census under-enumeration [@Cabral1995Migracio; @Santos2025Decolonizing]. Likewise, circular air travel between San Juan and the mainland United States makes Puerto Rican net migration highly volatile from year to year, amplifying inter-censal estimation drift prior to decennial census corrections [@USCensusPR2024; @Celade2019Observatorio].

Fourth, coarse 5-arc-minute gridded rasters inevitably blur narrow island littorals and indented bays. As audited in Table \ref{tab:raster-comparison}, coastal pixel masking inflates polygon footprint area from 200.416 km² surveyed land to 253.724 km² rasterised area and trims dense bayside pixels around Havana and San Juan, while administrative-regime transitions produce step discontinuities in the gridded time series prior to 1975. Authoritative demographic interpretation therefore anchors national and sub-regional headcounts to official census benchmarks while using the gridded layers strictly to visualise continuous spatial gradients.

# Conclusion

Between 1838 and 2025, the Greater Antilles experienced a nearly fifteenfold demographic expansion from roughly 2,72M to 40,2M inhabitants, yet diverged into five unmistakable modern demographic pathways shaped by emancipation timing, imperial integration, public-health reform and international migration [@Celade2020Observatorio; @Celade2024Observatorio]. Cuba led the archipelago for more than a century after 1841, swelling through early twentieth-century immigration and a sweeping health transition to 11,17M in 2012 before pioneer below-replacement fertility, rapid ageing and post-2015 emigration initiated structural decline [@USWarDeptCuba1900; @ONEICuba2014; @DiazBriquets1983; @Song2023Aging]. Puerto Rico compressed an even steeper rise and fall into a single century, peaking at 3,81M in 2000 before fiscal austerity and Hurricane María reduced its census population to 3,29M by 2020 [@VazquezCalzada1988; @Bureau2012Census; @USCensusPR2024]. Jamaica moderated its post-emancipation expansion through continuous diaspora outflows to Panama, Britain and North America, stabilising near 2,7M to 2,84M while shifting urban gravity into Kingston and Saint Catherine [@Roberts1957; @STATINJamaica2012; @Bourne2026Black].

The demographic centre of gravity of the entire archipelago consequently migrated onto Hispaniola. The Dominican Republic transformed from an underpopulated nineteenth-century ranching frontier of 135k inhabitants into an urbanised, economically diversified republic of 10,77M in 2022 led by Greater Santo Domingo (2,75M) and Santiago de los Caballeros (612,6k) [@MoyaPons1995; @ONEDomRep2023]. Haiti climbed from roughly 380k post-revolutionary survivors in 1805 and 3,1M in 1950 to 10,91M by 2015 and near 11,9M by 2025, coupling the Caribbean's highest rural density with rapid metropolitan agglomeration across Port-au-Prince and its neighbouring communes [@IHSIHaiti2015]. Together, the 292 catalogued settlements and 25 sub-administrative census benchmarks trace how a single tropical island arc simultaneously houses the Western Hemisphere's fastest-ageing contracting societies and its last major cohort of young demographic growth.
